newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Analysts' views on Brazil May interest rate.
newsitem.headline: Analysts' views on Brazil May interest rate.

text.p: Following are economists reactions to the Brazilian Central Bank's decision to keep its basic interest rate for May at the same level as April's 1.58 percent, which reversed a six-month policy of cutting rates by 4 basis points a month.

ROBERTO PADOVANI, economist at Trend Analise: "This is a good sign because it sends a signal that the Central Bank is also worrying about the external accounts and what could happen with the trade deficit. The Central Bank is also worried about economic activity in Brazil and the threat of U.S. interest rate hikes."
Padovani, however, said it was unlikely that the Central Bank had decided to completely end its policy of gradual rate reductions, saying it could resume cuts next month.
"They take these decisions based on conditions each month. They could lower it again next month," he said.

MARCELO AUDI, chief economist for Merrill Lynch in Brazil: "This was not expected but I view it as a positive and prudent measure to have more control over the current account deficit. It is also in line with expectations that the government, maybe in the short term, could adopt more restrictive credit measures," he said.
Brazil's trade deficit is expected to grow to about $10 billion this year, from $5.5 billion in 1996, which is seen pushing the 1997 current account gap above $30 billion.
MARCELO ALLAIN, chief economist at Banco BMC: "Half of the market was expecting a four basis point cut and the other half was looking for a two basis point cut so this was a surprise.

"I think the Central Bank wanted to send the market a signal that it would not allow the exchange coupon (the spread differential in current interest rates and exchange rate depreciation) to fall much further," Allain said.
The exchange coupon, effectively the rate of return for foreign investors in Brazilian fixed income securities, has fallen to about 10 percent from above 20 percent at the end of 1995, Allain said.
